title: Independence Day and the idea of Rashtra hit
author: Editorial Desk
summary: What it means to put the nation first in a workplace.
body:
On 15 August, the nation remembers those who gave their lives for freedom. For a trade union that puts **Rashtra hit**, the national interest, first in its three-part motto, it is also a day to ask what nation-first means on the shop floor. This post looks at the idea as BMS states it, the constitutional promises to workers that independence brought, and why asking for workers' rights and serving the nation are, in BMS's view, the same task.

## The motto and where it comes from

BMS's motto is *Rashtrahit, Udyogahit, Shramikahit*: the interest of the nation, of the industry and of the worker, in that order. Its English form reads "Nationalise the Labour, Labourise the Industry, Industrialise the Nation". Its founder, Dattopant Thengadi, started BMS in Bhopal in 1955, eight years after independence, with the view that Indian labour should be organised on Indian lines instead of by borrowing the idea of class war from abroad. BMS's own pages say it rejects the Marxist theory of class struggle, but opposes injustice and exploitation wherever they occur. Its slogans include "Bharat Mata ki Jai" and "Produce maximum, consume with restraint".

## Three practical meanings

- **Production.** A worker who produces well strengthens national output. BMS's stated aim is maximum production with equitable distribution: productivity is a duty of the worker, and a fair share is the worker's right. The two are meant to go together, and neither is conditional on the other.
- **Honesty.** Avoiding corruption and waste in public enterprises. Public sector units belong to the nation, and workers have an interest in their survival.
- **Self-reliance.** Buying and building at home where possible. BMS favours swadeshi products and self-reliant technology, and Thengadi was closely associated with the Swadeshi Jagran Manch, which took shape in 1991.

## What it does not mean

It does not mean silence about grievances. BMS asks for what it considers workers' rights through memoranda and demonstrations, as the nationwide Demands Day of 17 August 2026, just two days after Independence Day, showed. On that day it called for a higher minimum pension under EPS-95, restoration of the Old Pension Scheme, higher wage ceilings for provident fund and insurance coverage, better honoraria for scheme workers, equal pay for contract workers and amendments to the new Labour Codes, among other things. BMS also holds that strikes should be a last resort after negotiation fails, and that violence has no place in them. Its principle of "responsive cooperation" asks it to judge each policy of an elected government on merit, not on the party colour of the government. Thengadi, according to a biographical page, refused to make BMS an affiliate of the Janata Party after the Emergency, and BMS today says it has no tie to any political party.

## What independence promised workers

The Constitution adopted in 1950 contained promises to workers in its Directive Principles. Article 43 asks the State to endeavour to secure for all workers a living wage and conditions of work that ensure a decent standard of life, and to promote cottage industries in rural areas. When the Constituent Assembly debated the draft on 23 November 1948, members argued that economic and social democracy were conditions for political democracy and that cottage industries should be built on cooperative lines.

Article 43A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment in 1976 and in force from 3 January 1977, asks the State to take steps to secure workers' participation in the management of industrial undertakings. It is a directive and not an enforceable right. A Bill on the subject introduced in 1990 was not enacted, and India has no general central law on it, so progress has come through voluntary schemes and, to a limited extent, through the Industrial Relations Code, which mainly adds consultation. The Supreme Court has used Article 43A in some cases, for example to hold that workers could be heard in a winding-up petition in 1983, and has held in another that it gives no right to be consulted before a disinvestment decision. The gap between the promise and the practice is exactly where unions work.

## Workers in the freedom movement

Industrial workers were part of the freedom struggle. In July 1908, after Lokmanya Tilak was convicted of sedition, more than 100,000 Bombay textile workers shut down the city's mills in a six-day strike, according to one historical summary, which adds that Lenin took note of it as a sign of a new political force. Textile workers' unions in Bombay also struck during the First World War over bonus and during the 1920s over hours and mill rationalisation. The history of labour and the history of the national movement overlap, and descendants of those workers still work in the textile industry today. Accounts differ on the details of each strike, and readers who want to study them should consult primary and academic sources.

## The self-employed and the unorganised

Thengadi noted that a large part of the nation's work is done not by employees but by self-employed artisans, such as goldsmiths, potters, tailors and barbers. BMS says it was the first central trade union to recognise this "Vishwakarma sector", which it describes as a people's sector, neither private nor public. For a union that speaks of the nation, this sector is part of the answer to the question "which workers?" The same applies to scheme workers. BMS says there are more than a crore of them, working in schemes such as Anganwadi and mid-day meals, and argues that most are skilled but are not recognised as workers. The Anganwadi scheme, it points out, began in October 1975.

## A closing thought

Freedom has a meaning at work: wages paid on time, safe workplaces and a voice. For BMS, Independence Day is a moment to ask whether those things have reached the last worker. The task of making them real, through production, honest management, fair pay and a respectful hearing, is the unfinished work of independence, and BMS asks that it be done in the name of the nation and not against it.
